questions.q: A single qubit shows a 2.34% observed error rate against an expected 0%. The error was actually injected as a gate-level X-error right before measurement. Could you tell this from readout error using only the final counts?
options: Yes, gate error always produces a different count pattern than readout error
No — for a single qubit measured once per shot, a gate error applied right before measurement and a pure readout error are statistically indistinguishable from counts alone
Yes, but only if you run more than 10,000 shots
No, because gate error never actually affects measurement counts
questions.explain: Both a late gate error and a pure readout error distort the final measured outcome in the same statistical way, so the counts alone can't reveal which one occurred — a separate characterization experiment is needed to isolate the measurement step.

questions.q: What tool from the readout-mitigation lesson would you actually need to run to isolate readout error from gate error?
options: A visualization tool like `qiskit.visualization.plot_histogram`
A dedicated characterization experiment, such as `LocalReadoutError`, that specifically isolates the measurement step
Running the exact same circuit again with more shots
Switching from Qiskit Aer to a different simulator
questions.explain: Characterization experiments like LocalReadoutError are designed specifically to measure the readout step in isolation from the rest of the circuit, which is the only way to separately attribute error to readout versus gates.

questions.q: Applying M⁻¹ = [[1.021053, -0.031579], [-0.021053, 1.031579]] to an observed vector [0.60, 0.40] gives a corrected vector. What property must any valid corrected probability vector satisfy, regardless of the specific numbers?
options: Its two entries must be equal to each other
Its two entries must sum to 1
Its two entries must both be greater than 0.5
Its two entries must match the original observed vector exactly
questions.explain: Since the entries represent P(0) and P(1) for a single qubit, a correctly computed corrected vector must sum to 1, just like any valid probability distribution — a quick sanity check on the arithmetic.

questions.q: Using the linear teaching model, extrapolating from E(1)=0.72 and E(3)=0.56 via E(0) = (3·E(1) − E(3)) / 2 gives what result, and why does it match the result from using E(1) and E(2)?
options: 0.64; it differs because different point pairs always give different answers
0.80; it matches because the underlying data was constructed to be exactly linear, so any valid pair of points extrapolates to the same zero-noise estimate
0.56; it matches because E(3) is always the correct answer
1.28; it differs because real hardware noise is never linear
questions.explain: (3(0.72) − 0.56)/2 = 0.80, the same value obtained using E(1) and E(2), because the teaching model's noise was deliberately constructed as an exactly linear function of λ, so any two points on that line extrapolate to the same intercept.

questions.q: What is the central lesson this lab is building toward about error mitigation techniques like readout correction and ZNE?
options: They physically eliminate noise from the quantum hardware itself
They improve a reported estimate using known error structure from multiple imperfect measurements, without removing the real noise present on every actual run
They only work in simulation and have no real-hardware equivalent
They make readout error and gate error indistinguishable on purpose
questions.explain: Both readout correction and ZNE work by combining and reasoning about multiple imperfect measurements to produce a better final estimate — the underlying hardware noise is still present on every real run; what improves is how much of it survives into the reported number.
